claim: Estrogen receptor alpha (ERα) activation by estrogens prevents atheroma through its nuclear action.
source: Estrogen receptor alpha (ERα) activation by estrogens prevents atheroma through its nuclear action, whereas plasma membrane-located ERα accelerates endothelial healing.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a known fact about ERα function.

claim: Plasma membrane-located ERα accelerates endothelial healing.
source: Estrogen receptor alpha (ERα) activation by estrogens prevents atheroma through its nuclear action, whereas plasma membrane-located ERα accelerates endothelial healing.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a known fact about membrane ERα function.

claim: The genetic deficiency of ERα was associated with a reduction in flow-mediated dilation (FMD) in one man.
source: The genetic deficiency of ERα was associated with a reduction in flow-mediated dilation (FMD) in one man.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and refers to a clinical observation.

claim: FMD was reduced in male and female mice lacking ERα (Esr1-/- mice) compared to wild-type mice.
source: FMD, but not agonist (acetylcholine, insulin)-mediated dilation, was reduced in male and female mice lacking ERα (Esr1-/- mice) compared to wild-type mice and was not dependent on the presence of estrogens.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study presented in the abstract and supported by data in Figure 1.

claim: Agonist-mediated dilation (acetylcholine, insulin) was not reduced in Esr1-/- mice compared to wild-type mice.
source: FMD, but not agonist (acetylcholine, insulin)-mediated dilation, was reduced in male and female mice lacking ERα (Esr1-/- mice) compared to wild-type mice and was not dependent on the presence of estrogens.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by data in Figure 1E-G.

claim: The reduction in FMD in Esr1-/- mice was not dependent on the presence of estrogens.
source: FMD, but not agonist (acetylcholine, insulin)-mediated dilation, was reduced in male and female mice lacking ERα (Esr1-/- mice) compared to wild-type mice and was not dependent on the presence of estrogens.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by experiments with ovariectomized mice and exogenous estrogen treatments.

claim: FMD was reduced in C451A-ERα mice lacking membrane ERα.
source: In C451A-ERα mice lacking membrane ERα, not in mice lacking AF2-dependent nuclear ERα actions, FMD was reduced, and restored by antioxidant treatments.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by data in Figure 3G.

claim: FMD was not reduced in mice lacking AF2-dependent nuclear ERα actions.
source: In C451A-ERα mice lacking membrane ERα, not in mice lacking AF2-dependent nuclear ERα actions, FMD was reduced, and restored by antioxidant treatments.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by data in Figure 3C.

claim: FMD in C451A-ERα mice was restored by antioxidant treatments.
source: In C451A-ERα mice lacking membrane ERα, not in mice lacking AF2-dependent nuclear ERα actions, FMD was reduced, and restored by antioxidant treatments.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by data in Figures 7 and 8.

claim: Isolated perfused kidneys of C451A-ERα mice revealed a decreased flow-mediated nitrate production compared to wild-type mice.
source: Compared to wild-type mice, isolated perfused kidneys of C451A-ERα mice revealed a decreased flow-mediated nitrate production and an increased H2O2 production.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by data in Figure 6D.

claim: Isolated perfused kidneys of C451A-ERα mice revealed an increased H2O2 production compared to wild-type mice.
source: Compared to wild-type mice, isolated perfused kidneys of C451A-ERα mice revealed a decreased flow-mediated nitrate production and an increased H2O2 production.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by data in Figure 6F.

claim: Endothelial membrane ERα promotes NO bioavailability through inhibition of oxidative stress.
source: Thus, endothelial membrane ERα promotes NO bioavailability through inhibition of oxidative stress and thereby participates in FMD in a ligand-independent manner.
evidence: This is the main conclusion stated in the abstract, based on the experimental findings.

claim: Endothelial membrane ERα participates in FMD in a ligand-independent manner.
source: Thus, endothelial membrane ERα promotes NO bioavailability through inhibition of oxidative stress and thereby participates in FMD in a ligand-independent manner.
evidence: This is the main conclusion stated in the abstract, based on experiments showing no effect of exogenous estrogens and similar FMD in intact and ovariectomized mice.

claim: FMD measured in the human forearm depends mainly on the acute production of NO by endothelial cells in response to an acute increase in shear stress.
source: FMD measured in the human forearm depends mainly on the acute production of NO by endothelial cells in response to an acute increase in shear stress (Joannides et al., 1995; Green et al., 2014; Zhou et al., 2014) and reduced FMD is a hallmark of endothelium dysfunction (Zhou et al., 2014; Rizzoni and Agabiti Rosei, 2006; Stoner and Sabatier, 2012).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: Reduced FMD is a hallmark of endothelium dysfunction.
source: FMD measured in the human forearm depends mainly on the acute production of NO by endothelial cells in response to an acute increase in shear stress (Joannides et al., 1995; Green et al., 2014; Zhou et al., 2014) and reduced FMD is a hallmark of endothelium dysfunction (Zhou et al., 2014; Rizzoni and Agabiti Rosei, 2006; Stoner and Sabatier, 2012).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: Prior to menopause, women are less affected by cardiovascular disorders than men.
source: Epidemiological investigations have shown that, prior to menopause, women are less affected by cardiovascular disorders than men (Simoncini, 2009; Arnal et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: Estrogens protect against atherosclerosis.
source: Estrogens protect against atherosclerosis (Billon-Galés et al., 2009) and neointimal proliferation (Smirnova et al., 2015), and accelerate re-endothelialization of injured arteries (Brouchet et al., 2001).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: Estrogens protect against neointimal proliferation.
source: Estrogens protect against atherosclerosis (Billon-Galés et al., 2009) and neointimal proliferation (Smirnova et al., 2015), and accelerate re-endothelialization of injured arteries (Brouchet et al., 2001).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: Estrogens accelerate re-endothelialization of injured arteries.
source: Estrogens protect against atherosclerosis (Billon-Galés et al., 2009) and neointimal proliferation (Smirnova et al., 2015), and accelerate re-endothelialization of injured arteries (Brouchet et al., 2001).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: E2 and ERα, and more precisely its nuclear activating function AF2, are both essential for the arterial outward remodeling induced by a chronic rise in blood flow in vivo.
source: Indeed, we have previously shown that E2 and ERα, and more precisely its nuclear activating function AF2, are both essential for the arterial outward remodeling induced by a chronic rise in blood flow in vivo (Tarhouni et al., 2013; Tarhouni et al., 2014a; Tarhouni et al., 2014b).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations to previous work by the authors.

claim: A subpopulation of ERα is associated with the plasma membrane and activates non-nuclear signaling.
source: However, a subpopulation of ERα is also associated with the plasma membrane and activates non-nuclear signaling (Arnal et al., 2017; Banerjee et al., 2014; Lu et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: The acute effect initially described in 1967 was a rapid increase in AMPc production in the rat uterus in response to E2.
source: The acute effect initially described in 1967 was a rapid increase in AMPc production in the rat uterus in response to E2 (Szego and Davis, 1967).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a supporting citation.

claim: E2 binding to the plasma membrane was reported in endometrial cells and hepatocytes.
source: E2 binding to the plasma membrane was subsequently reported in endometrial cells and hepatocytes (Pietras and Szego, 1977), suggesting that a fraction of ERα could be located to the membrane and contributes to the rapid effects of E2, possibly through the rapid activation of G proteins and kinases such as ERK1-2, PI3K, or P21ras (Arnal et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: In ovine fetal pulmonary artery endothelial cells, E2 stimulates eNOS activity through activation of ERα leading to increased intracellular Ca2+ within minutes.
source: In ovine fetal pulmonary artery endothelial cells, E2 stimulates eNOS activity through activation of ERα leading to increased intracellular Ca2+ within minutes (Lantin-Hermoso et al., 1997).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a supporting citation.

claim: In HUVECs, E2 induces a rapid production of NO and cGMP independent of an increase in intracellular Ca2+.
source: By contrast, in HUVECs, E2 induces a rapid production of NO and cGMP independent of an increase in intracellular Ca2+ (Caulin-Glaser et al., 1997).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a supporting citation.

claim: The rapid nongenomic activation of eNOS involves Akt/PKB.
source: This rapid nongenomic activation of eNOS involves Akt/PKB (Florian et al., 2004) and MAP kinase-dependent mechanisms (Chen et al., 1999).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: The rapid nongenomic activation of eNOS involves MAP kinase-dependent mechanisms.
source: This rapid nongenomic activation of eNOS involves Akt/PKB (Florian et al., 2004) and MAP kinase-dependent mechanisms (Chen et al., 1999).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: Estradiol-induced endothelium-independent dilation was described in canine coronary arteries.
source: Estradiol-induced endothelium-independent dilation was also described in canine coronary arteries (Sudhir et al., 1995) and in rat cerebral microvessels (Florian et al., 2004).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: Estradiol-induced endothelium-independent dilation was described in rat cerebral microvessels.
source: Estradiol-induced endothelium-independent dilation was also described in canine coronary arteries (Sudhir et al., 1995) and in rat cerebral microvessels (Florian et al., 2004).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: The acute vasodilator effect of E2 is mediated by membrane-associated ERα.
source: Using a mouse model lacking membrane-associated ERα, we demonstrated that the acute vasodilator effect of E2 and its accelerative effect on re-endothelialization are mediated by membrane-associated ERα (Adlanmerini et al., 2014; Zahreddine et al., 2021).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations to previous work by the authors.

claim: The accelerative effect of E2 on re-endothelialization is mediated by membrane-associated ERα.
source: Using a mouse model lacking membrane-associated ERα, we demonstrated that the acute vasodilator effect of E2 and its accelerative effect on re-endothelialization are mediated by membrane-associated ERα (Adlanmerini et al., 2014; Zahreddine et al., 2021).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations to previous work by the authors.

claim: E2 exerts protective effects against atheroma, angiotensin 2-induced hypertension, and neointimal hyperplasia through its nuclear effects.
source: On the other hand, E2 exerts protective effects against atheroma, angiotensin 2-induced hypertension, and neointimal hyperplasia through its nuclear effects (Guivarc'h et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a supporting citation.

claim: GPER is located not only at the plasma membrane but also on the membrane of the endoplasmic reticulum.
source: The 7-transmembrane G-protein-coupled estrogen receptor (GPER, formerly known as GPR30) is another receptor located not only at the plasma membrane but also on the membrane of the endoplasmic reticulum that can be activated by E2.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as background information.

claim: GPER can be activated by E2.
source: The 7-transmembrane G-protein-coupled estrogen receptor (GPER, formerly known as GPR30) is another receptor located not only at the plasma membrane but also on the membrane of the endoplasmic reticulum that can be activated by E2.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as background information.

claim: GPER was found in both human and animal arteries.
source: It was found in both human and animal arteries (Prossnitz and Barton, 2011; Barton et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: In the rat, GPER activation by its agonist G-1 reduces uterine vascular tone during pregnancy through activation of endothelium-dependent NO production.
source: In the rat, GPER activation by its agonist G-1 reduces uterine vascular tone during pregnancy through activation of endothelium-dependent NO production (Tropea et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a supporting citation.

claim: The G-1-induced relaxation of the mesenteric resistance arteries in both male and female rats is mainly mediated by the PI3K-Akt-eNOS pathway.
source: Likewise, the G-1-induced relaxation of the mesenteric resistance arteries in both male and female rats is mainly mediated by the PI3K-Akt-eNOS pathway (Peixoto et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a supporting citation.

claim: GPER partly contributes to E2-dependent vasodilation of mouse aortae.
source: Noteworthy, GPER partly contributes to E2-dependent vasodilation of mouse aortae (Fredette et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a supporting citation.

claim: Endothelium-dependent dilation of subcutaneous arteries is reduced in post-menopausal women compared to pre-menopausal women.
source: For instance, endothelium-dependent dilation of subcutaneous arteries is reduced in post-menopausal women compared to pre-menopausal women (Kublickiene et al., 2005; Kublickiene et al., 2008).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: Diet phytoestrogens could have protective actions in postmenopausal women suffering coronary artery disease.
source: Similarly, diet phytoestrogens could have protective actions in postmenopausal women suffering coronary artery disease (Cruz et al., 2008) and selective estrogen receptor modulators (SERMs) such as raloxifene exert protective actions in female rats through eNOS activation (Chan et al., 2010).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a supporting citation.

claim: Selective estrogen receptor modulators (SERMs) such as raloxifene exert protective actions in female rats through eNOS activation.
source: Similarly, diet phytoestrogens could have protective actions in postmenopausal women suffering coronary artery disease (Cruz et al., 2008) and selective estrogen receptor modulators (SERMs) such as raloxifene exert protective actions in female rats through eNOS activation (Chan et al., 2010).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a supporting citation.

claim: Hormonal replacement therapy activates endothelium-derived hyperpolarizing factor (EDHF)-mediated vasodilation in rat mesenteric and uterine arteries.
source: Besides the activation of eNOS, hormonal replacement therapy also activates endothelium-derived hyperpolarizing factor (EDHF)-mediated vasodilation as shown in rat mesenteric and uterine arteries (Burger et al., 2009) as well as in the rat gracilis muscle artery with increased Epoxyeicosatrienoic acids (EETs) production involved in E2-mediated increase in FMD in hypertensive or old rats (Huang et al., 2001; Sun et al., 2004).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: Increased Epoxyeicosatrienoic acids (EETs) production is involved in E2-mediated increase in FMD in hypertensive or old rats.
source: Besides the activation of eNOS, hormonal replacement therapy also activates endothelium-derived hyperpolarizing factor (EDHF)-mediated vasodilation as shown in rat mesenteric and uterine arteries (Burger et al., 2009) as well as in the rat gracilis muscle artery with increased Epoxyeicosatrienoic acids (EETs) production involved in E2-mediated increase in FMD in hypertensive or old rats (Huang et al., 2001; Sun et al., 2004).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: Estrogen therapy reduces pressure (myogenic) contraction.
source: Furthermore, estrogen therapy reduces pressure (myogenic) (Kublickiene et al., 2005; Kublickiene et al., 2008) and adrenergic-dependent contraction (Meyer et al., 1997).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: Estrogen therapy reduces adrenergic-dependent contraction.
source: Furthermore, estrogen therapy reduces pressure (myogenic) (Kublickiene et al., 2005; Kublickiene et al., 2008) and adrenergic-dependent contraction (Meyer et al., 1997).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: FMD is improved by E2 in rat gracilis muscle arteries.
source: FMD is also improved by E2 in rat gracilis muscle arteries (Huang et al., 1998).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a supporting citation.

claim: There is an increase in the amplitude of FMD in women among the menstrual cycle with a greater dilation during the luteal or follicular phase.
source: Although there is an increase in the amplitude of FMD in women among the menstrual cycle with a greater dilation during the luteal or follicular phase (Hashimoto et al., 1995), FMD is similar in healthy young men and women (Sullivan et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: FMD is similar in healthy young men and women.
source: Although there is an increase in the amplitude of FMD in women among the menstrual cycle with a greater dilation during the luteal or follicular phase (Hashimoto et al., 1995), FMD is similar in healthy young men and women (Sullivan et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a supporting citation.

claim: The first disruptive mutation in the gene encoding ERα, reported in 1994 in a man who was only 30 years old, was found to be associated with a total absence of FMD.
source: Importantly, the first disruptive mutation in the gene encoding ERα, reported in 1994 in a man who was only 30 years old (Smith et al., 1994), was found to be associated with a total absence of FMD (Sudhir et al., 1997).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: Conversion of testosterone into estradiol by aromatase which is expressed in the arterial wall has been shown to reduce early atherogenesis in male mice.
source: Of note, conversion of testosterone into estradiol by aromatase which is expressed in the arterial wall has been shown to reduce early atherogenesis in male mice (Nathan et al., 2001).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a supporting citation.

claim: Precontraction prior to FMD was not significantly affected by the absence of ERα in Esr1-/- mice.
source: Precontraction prior to FMD (Figure 1C) and arterial diameter (Figure 1D) were not significantly affected by the absence of ERα.
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by data in Figure 1C.

claim: Arterial diameter was not significantly affected by the absence of ERα in Esr1-/- mice.
source: Precontraction prior to FMD (Figure 1C) and arterial diameter (Figure 1D) were not significantly affected by the absence of ERα.
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by data in Figure 1D.

claim: Agonist-mediated endothelium-dependent (acetylcholine and insulin) and endothelium-independent (SNP) dilation were not significantly affected by the absence of ERα in Esr1-/- mice.
source: Agonist-mediated endothelium-dependent (acetylcholine and insulin) and endothelium-independent (SNP) dilation were not significantly affected by the absence of ERα (Figure 1E–G).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by data in Figure 1E-G.

claim: Exogenous E2 did not affect FMD in mesenteric resistance arteries isolated from male WT mice after 20 min incubation.
source: To directly investigate the influence of estrogens on FMD, mesenteric resistance arteries isolated from male WT mice were incubated (20 min) with E2, which activates both membrane-associated and nuclear ERα, or with another natural estrogen, estetrol (E4), which activates only nuclear ERα (Abot et al., 2014). These exogenous estrogens did not affect FMD (Figure 1H).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by data in Figure 1H.

claim: Exogenous E4 did not affect FMD in mesenteric resistance arteries isolated from male WT mice after 20 min incubation.
source: To directly investigate the influence of estrogens on FMD, mesenteric resistance arteries isolated from male WT mice were incubated (20 min) with E2, which activates both membrane-associated and nuclear ERα, or with another natural estrogen, estetrol (E4), which activates only nuclear ERα (Abot et al., 2014). These exogenous estrogens did not affect FMD (Figure 1H).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by data in Figure 1H.

claim: E4 activates only nuclear ERα.
source: To directly investigate the influence of estrogens on FMD, mesenteric resistance arteries isolated from male WT mice were incubated (20 min) with E2, which activates both membrane-associated and nuclear ERα, or with another natural estrogen, estetrol (E4), which activates only nuclear ERα (Abot et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated in the results section with a supporting citation.

claim: ICI-182780 did not alter FMD after 20 min of incubation with isolated arteries.
source: Furthermore, the estrogen receptor downregulator and GPER agonist fulvestrant (ICI-182780) (Meyer et al., 2010; Jacenik et al., 2016) did not alter FMD after 20 min of incubation with isolated arteries (Figure 1H).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by data in Figure 1H.

claim: FMD in mesenteric resistance arteries was similarly reduced in both intact and ovariectomized female Esr1-/- mice compared to their respective Esr1+/+ littermate controls.
source: We also found that FMD in mesenteric resistance arteries was similarly reduced in both intact (Figure 1K) and ovariectomized female Esr1-/- mice (Figure 1L) compared to their respective Esr1+/+ littermate controls.
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by data in Figure 1K and 1L.

claim: FMD was similar in intact and ovariectomized female WT mice.
source: The similar levels of FMD in intact and ovariectomized female WT mice, as well as in male mice, suggest that circulating endogenous estrogens do not influence FMD in young healthy mice.
evidence: This is inferred from the comparison of FMD levels in Figure 1K and 1L.

claim: Circulating endogenous estrogens do not influence FMD in young healthy mice.
source: The similar levels of FMD in intact and ovariectomized female WT mice, as well as in male mice, suggest that circulating endogenous estrogens do not influence FMD in young healthy mice.
evidence: This is stated in the results section based on the comparison of FMD in different groups.

claim: FMD was reduced in the uterine artery isolated from female Esr1-/- mice in comparison with Esr1+/+ mice.
source: FMD was also reduced in the uterine artery isolated from female Esr1-/- mice in comparison with Esr1+/+ mice (Figure 1M).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by data in Figure 1M.

claim: FMD was not altered by the inactivation of Esr2, encoding ERβ in mice.
source: FMD was not altered by the inactivation of Esr2, encoding ERβ in mice (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by data in Figure 2A.

claim: Arterial precontraction, basal diameter and acetylcholine-mediated dilation were not significantly affected by the absence of ERβ.
source: Similarly, arterial precontraction, basal diameter and acetylcholine-mediated dilation were not significantly affected by the absence of ERß (Figure 2B–D).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by data in Figure 2B-D.

claim: FMD was reduced in arteries isolated from TekCre/+: Esr1f/f mice (lacking endothelial ERα) compared to littermate WT mice.
source: As FMD depends on the response of the endothelium to shear stress, we next investigated FMD in mice lacking ERα in endothelial cells (TekCre/+: Esr1f/f mice). FMD was reduced in arteries isolated from these mice compared to littermate WT mice (Figure 2E).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by data in Figure 2E.

claim: Arterial precontraction, basal diameter and acetylcholine-mediated dilation were not significantly affected by the absence of endothelial ERα in TekCre/+: Esr1f/f mice.
source: Arterial precontraction, basal diameter and acetylcholine-mediated dilation were not significantly affected by the absence of endothelial ERα (Figure 2F–H).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by data in Figure 2F-H.

claim: The gene expression level of Esr1 (encoding ERα) in endothelial cells was not affected by invalidation of the AF2 function of ERα.
source: The gene expression level of Esr1 (encoding ERα) in endothelial cells was not affected by invalidation of the AF2 function of ERα (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by data in Figure 3B.

claim: FMD was not significantly reduced in mesenteric resistance arteries isolated from AF20ERα male mice compared to littermate AF20WT animals.
source: We observed that FMD was not significantly reduced in mesenteric resistance arteries isolated from AF20ERα male mice compared to littermate AF20WT animals (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by data in Figure 3C.

claim: Acetylcholine-mediated dilation was not altered by loss of the nuclear AF2 function of ERα.
source: Acetylcholine-mediated dilation (Figure 3D) was not altered by loss of the nuclear AF2 function of ERα.
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by data in Figure 3D.

claim: FMD was preserved despite the loss of AF2 nuclear function of ERα.
source: Thus, we demonstrated that FMD was preserved despite the loss of AF2 nuclear function of ERα.
evidence: This is stated in the results section as a conclusion from the AF20ERα experiments.

claim: The gene expression level of Esr1 was not significantly altered in aortic endothelial cells isolated from C451A-ERα mice compared to wild-type mice.
source: The gene expression level of Esr1 was not significantly altered in aortic endothelial cells isolated from C451A-ERα mice compared to wild-type mice (Figure 3F).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by data in Figure 3F.

claim: FMD was significantly reduced in C451A-ERα mice compared to WT littermate animals.
source: FMD was significantly reduced compared to WT littermate animals (Figure 3G) while acetylcholine-mediated dilation was not significantly affected by the absence of membrane-associated ERα (Figure 3H).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by data in Figure 3G.

claim: Acetylcholine-mediated dilation was not significantly affected by the absence of membrane-associated ERα in C451A-ERα mice.
source: FMD was significantly reduced compared to WT littermate animals (Figure 3G) while acetylcholine-mediated dilation was not significantly affected by the absence of membrane-associated ERα (Figure 3H).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by data in Figure 3H.

claim: The gene expression level of Esr1 was not significantly altered in aortic endothelial cells isolated from R264A-ERα mice compared to wild-type mice.
source: The gene expression level of Esr1 was not significantly altered in aortic endothelial cells isolated from R264A-ERα mice compared to wild-type mice (Figure 3J).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by data in Figure 3J.

claim: FMD was significantly reduced in R264A-ERα male mice compared to WT littermate controls.
source: We found that FMD was significantly reduced in R264A-ERα male mice compared to WT littermate controls (Figure 3K).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by data in Figure 3K.

claim: Acetylcholine-mediated dilation was not significantly affected by the absence of membrane-associated ERα effects in R264A-ERα male mice.
source: On the other hand, acetylcholine-mediated dilation was not significantly affected by the absence of membrane-associated ERα effects in R264A-ERα male mice (Figure 3L).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by data in Figure 3L.

claim: FMD was altered as a consequence of either the inactivation of palmitoylation site of ERα (C451A-ERα mice) or the impairment of the activation of the Gαi protein by ERα (R264A-ERα mice).
source: Thus, we demonstrated that FMD was altered as a consequence of either the inactivation of palmitoylation site of ERα (C451A-ERα mice) or the impairment of the activation of the Gαi protein by ERα (R264A-ERα mice), thus preventing membrane-associated ERα activation of FMD in male mice.
evidence: This is stated in the results section as a conclusion from the C451A-ERα and R264A-ERα experiments.

claim: FMD was significantly reduced by L-NNA in mesenteric resistance arteries of the four groups of littermate WT mice.
source: FMD was significantly reduced by L-NNA in mesenteric resistance arteries of the four groups of littermate WT mice (Figure 4A–D), whereas L-NNA had no significant effect on FMD in Esr1-/- (Figure 4A), C451A-ERα (Figure 4B), and R264A-ERα mice (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by data in Figure 4A-D.

claim: L-NNA had no significant effect on FMD in Esr1-/- mice.
source: FMD was significantly reduced by L-NNA in mesenteric resistance arteries of the four groups of littermate WT mice (Figure 4A–D), whereas L-NNA had no significant effect on FMD in Esr1-/- (Figure 4A), C451A-ERα (Figure 4B), and R264A-ERα mice (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by data in Figure 4A.

claim: L-NNA had no significant effect on FMD in C451A-ERα mice.
source: FMD was significantly reduced by L-NNA in mesenteric resistance arteries of the four groups of littermate WT mice (Figure 4A–D), whereas L-NNA had no significant effect on FMD in Esr1-/- (Figure 4A), C451A-ERα (Figure 4B), and R264A-ERα mice (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by data in Figure 4B.

claim: L-NNA had no significant effect on FMD in R264A-ERα mice.
source: FMD was significantly reduced by L-NNA in mesenteric resistance arteries of the four groups of littermate WT mice (Figure 4A–D), whereas L-NNA had no significant effect on FMD in Esr1-/- (Figure 4A), C451A-ERα (Figure 4B), and R264A-ERα mice (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by data in Figure 4C.

claim: FMD was reduced to a similar extent by L-NNA in AF20ERα and WT mice.
source: In contrast, FMD was reduced to a similar extent by L-NNA in AF20ERα and WT mice (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by data in Figure 4D.

claim: L-NNA strongly and similarly reduced acetylcholine-mediated relaxation in Esr1-/-, C451A-ERα, R264A-ERα, AF20ERα and the corresponding littermate WT mice.
source: L-NNA strongly and similarly reduced acetylcholine-mediated relaxation in Esr1-/- (Figure 4E), C451A-ERα (Figure 4F), R264A-ERα (Figure 4G), AF20ERα (Figure 4H) and the corresponding littermate WT mice (Figure 4E–H), thus showing that the alteration of membrane ERα activation affected selectively the flow-mediated NO-dependent dilation, but not the acetylcholine-mediated NO-dependent dilation.
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by data in Figure 4E-H.

claim: The alteration of membrane ERα activation affected selectively the flow-mediated NO-dependent dilation, but not the acetylcholine-mediated NO-dependent dilation.
source: L-NNA strongly and similarly reduced acetylcholine-mediated relaxation in Esr1-/- (Figure 4E), C451A-ERα (Figure 4F), R264A-ERα (Figure 4G), AF20ERα (Figure 4H) and the corresponding littermate WT mice (Figure 4E–H), thus showing that the alteration of membrane ERα activation affected selectively the flow-mediated NO-dependent dilation, but not the acetylcholine-mediated NO-dependent dilation.
evidence: This is stated in the results section as a conclusion from the L-NNA experiments.

claim: The addition of indomethacin did not further reduce FMD or acetylcholine-mediated relaxation in all the groups.

evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by data in Figure 4A-H.

claim: The addition of MSPPOH did not further reduce FMD or acetylcholine-mediated relaxation in all the groups.

evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by data in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A-F.

claim: In WT mice, the phosphorylation of eNOS at Ser1177 by flow (shear stress) was greater in arteries submitted to flow than in control (no flow) arteries.
source: In WT mice, the phosphorylation of eNOS at Ser1177 by flow (shear stress) was greater in arteries submitted to flow than in control (no flow) arteries as evidenced by a greater ratio of phosphorylated eNOS/total eNOS (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by data in Figure 5A.

claim: The ratio of phosphorylated eNOS/total eNOS was not significantly greater in arteries submitted to flow than in unstimulated arteries in C451A-ERα mice.
source: This ratio was not significantly greater in arteries submitted to flow than in unstimulated arteries in C451A-ERα mice (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by data in Figure 5A.

claim: The expression level of total eNOS was similar in C451A-ERα and in WT mice.
source: The expression level of total eNOS was similar in C451A-ERα and in WT mice (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by data in Figure 5B.

claim: A similar pattern of eNOS phosphorylation was observed in R264A-ERα mice as in C451A-ERα mice.
source: A similar pattern was observed in R264A-ERα mice (Figure 5D and E).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by data in Figure 5D and E.

claim: The ratio of phosphorylated eNOS/total eNOS was similarly increased by flow in WT and AF2-ERα mice.
source: By contrast, the ratio of phosphorylated eNOS/total eNOS was similarly increased by flow in WT and AF2-ERα mice without any change in total eNOS level between the two strains (Figure 5G and H).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by data in Figure 5G and H.

claim: There was no change in total eNOS level between WT and AF2-ERα mice.

evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by data in Figure 5G and H.

claim: The absence of membrane-associated ERα affects flow-mediated eNOS activation pathway, at least in part, by preventing the activation of its upstream activator Akt/PKB.

claim: The flow-pressure relationship was shifted leftward in C451A-ERα mice compared to WT mice in isolated perfused kidneys.

claim: Acetylcholine-mediated dilation in perfused kidneys was equivalent in C451A-ERα and WT mice.
source: Acetylcholine-mediated dilation in perfused kidneys was equivalent in C451A-ERα and WT mice (Figure 6C), suggesting that the response to flow was probably selectively reduced in perfused kidney of C451A-ERα mice, as shown above for the mesenteric artery.
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by data in Figure 6C.

claim: Phenylephrine-mediated contraction was not affected by the absence of membrane-ERα in perfused kidneys.
source: Similarly, phenylephrine-mediated contraction was not affected by the absence of membrane-ERα (51.1 ± 2.9 vs 57.4% ± 5.7% contraction, C451A-ERα and WT mice, n = 5 per group, p > 0.9999, Mann-Withney test).
evidence: This is stated in the results section with statistical analysis.

claim: Nitrate and nitrite concentration in the kidney perfusate was reduced in C451A-ERα compared to WT mice.
source: Then, we measured nitrate and nitrite concentration in the kidney perfusate and found that it was reduced in C451A-ERα compared to WT mice (Figure 6D).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by data in Figure 6D.

claim: ATP production measured in the kidney perfusate was reduced in C451A-ERα mice compared to WT mice.
source: Interestingly, ATP production measured in the kidney perfusate was also reduced in C451A-ERα mice (Figure 6E) whereas H2O2 production was higher in C451A-ERα than in WT mice (Figure 6F).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by data in Figure 6E.

claim: H2O2 production in the kidney perfusate was higher in C451A-ERα than in WT mice.
source: Interestingly, ATP production measured in the kidney perfusate was also reduced in C451A-ERα mice (Figure 6E) whereas H2O2 production was higher in C451A-ERα than in WT mice (Figure 6F).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by data in Figure 6F.

claim: No significant difference in gene expression of 44 genes involved in endothelial response to flow was observed between C451A-ERα and WT mice in mesenteric resistance arteries.
source: Finally, we analyzed in mesenteric resistance arteries the expression of 44 genes that may be involved in the rapid endothelial response to acute changes in flow (FMD). No significant difference was observed between C451A-ERα and WT mice (Figure 7—figure supplements 1 and 2), in line with the prominent or even exclusive role of rapid, non genomic, membrane-ERα.
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by data in Figure 7—figure supplements 1 and 2.

claim: The addition of PEG-SOD plus catalase to the bath containing mesenteric resistance arteries isolated from WT mice did not alter FMD.
source: First, the addition of PEG-SOD plus catalase to the bath containing mesenteric resistance arteries isolated from WT mice did not alter FMD (Figure 7A).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by data in Figure 7A.

claim: PEG-SOD plus catalase enhanced FMD in arteries from C451A-ERα mice.
source: By contrast, PEG-SOD plus catalase enhanced FMD in arteries from C451A-ERα mice (Figure 7B).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by data in Figure 7B.

claim: Catalase alone did not alter FMD in arteries from WT mice.
source: Catalase alone did not alter FMD in arteries from WT mice (Figure 7C), whereas it reduced FMD in arteries from C451A-ERα mice (Figure 7D).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by data in Figure 7C.

claim: Catalase alone reduced FMD in arteries from C451A-ERα mice.
source: Catalase alone did not alter FMD in arteries from WT mice (Figure 7C), whereas it reduced FMD in arteries from C451A-ERα mice (Figure 7D).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by data in Figure 7D.

claim: Inhibition of mitochondrial ROS production by Mito-Tempo did not affect FMD in arteries from WT mice.
source: Inhibition of mitochondrial ROS production by Mito-Tempo did not affect FMD in arteries from WT mice (Figure 7E), while it enhanced FMD in arteries isolated from C451A-ERα mice (Figure 7F).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by data in Figure 7E.

claim: Mito-Tempo enhanced FMD in arteries isolated from C451A-ERα mice.
source: Inhibition of mitochondrial ROS production by Mito-Tempo did not affect FMD in arteries from WT mice (Figure 7E), while it enhanced FMD in arteries isolated from C451A-ERα mice (Figure 7F).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by data in Figure 7F.

claim: The acute response to ATP was not affected by the absence of membrane ERα (C451A-ERα mice).

evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by data in Figure 7—figure supplement 3.

claim: The acute response to the Piezo1 agonist YODA-1 was not affected by the absence of membrane ERα (C451A-ERα mice).
source: The acute response to ATP and to the Piezo1 agonist YODA-1 were not affected by the absence of membrane ERα (C451A-ERα mice).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by data in Figure 7—figure supplement 3.

claim: The mechanosensitive channel blocker GsMTx4 similarly affected FMD in C451A-ERα and WT mice.
source: In addition, the mechanosensitive channel blocker GsMTx4 similarly affected FMD in C451A-ERα and WT mice, suggesting that the defect in FMD is located downstream flow sensing (Figure 7—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by data in Figure 7—figure supplement 3.

claim: The defect in FMD associated with the absence of membrane ERα is located downstream flow sensing.
source: In addition, the mechanosensitive channel blocker GsMTx4 similarly affected FMD in C451A-ERα and WT mice, suggesting that the defect in FMD is located downstream flow sensing (Figure 7—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is stated in the results section as an inference from the GsMTx4 experiments.

claim: Reactive oxygen species could reduce FMD in arteries from C451A-ERα mice.
source: This pharmacological approach suggests that reactive oxygen species could reduce FMD in arteries from C451A-ERα, while H2O2 could maintain in part the dilatory response induced by flow in the absence of membrane ERα.
evidence: This is stated in the results section as a conclusion from the antioxidant experiments.

claim: H2O2 could maintain in part the dilatory response induced by flow in the absence of membrane ERα.
source: This pharmacological approach suggests that reactive oxygen species could reduce FMD in arteries from C451A-ERα, while H2O2 could maintain in part the dilatory response induced by flow in the absence of membrane ERα.
evidence: This is stated in the results section as a conclusion from the antioxidant experiments.

claim: After 2 weeks of treatment with the antioxidant TEMPOL, there was no longer a discernible difference between the response of WT and C451A-ERα mice to flow.
source: After 2 weeks of treatment with the antioxidant TEMPOL, there was no longer a discernible difference between the response of WT and C451A-ERα mice to flow (Figure 8A).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by data in Figure 8A.

claim: Mice body weight, arterial diameter, phenylephrine-, and KCl-mediated contraction as well as acetylcholine-mediated dilation were not different between TEMPOL-treated WT and C451A-ERα mice.
source: Mice body weight, arterial diameter, phenylephrine-, and KCl-mediated contraction as well as acetylcholine-mediated dilation were not different between TEMPOL-treated WT and C451A-ERα mice (Figure 8B–F).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by data in Figure 8B-F.

claim: A similar pattern of FMD normalization was observed in mice treated for 4 weeks with vitamin E and vitamin C.
source: A similar pattern was observed in mice treated for 4 weeks with vitamin E and vitamin C with no difference in FMD between WT and C451A-ERα mice (Figure 8G to L).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by data in Figure 8G-L.

claim: Antioxidant treatment normalized FMD in C451A-ERα mice to the level of FMD in WT mice.
source: Thus, antioxidant treatment normalized FMD in C451A-ERα mice to the level of FMD in WT mice.
evidence: This is stated in the results section as a conclusion from the in vivo antioxidant treatment experiments.

claim: The absence of membrane-associated ERα increases oxidative stress, which in turn could be responsible for a large part of the alteration of NO-dependent FMD.
source: Altogether, these data suggest that the absence of membrane-associated ERα increases oxidative stress, which in turn could be responsible for a large part of the alteration of NO-dependent FMD.
evidence: This is stated in the results section as a conclusion from all the antioxidant experiments.

claim: Endothelial membrane-associated ERα contributed to optimize flow (shear stress)-mediated dilation in young healthy mouse resistance arteries in a ligand-independent manner.
source: We report here that endothelial membrane-associated ERα contributed to optimize flow (shear stress)-mediated dilation in young healthy mouse resistance arteries in a ligand-independent manner.
evidence: This is the main conclusion stated in the discussion section.

claim: FMD involves unliganded ERα activation in response to shear stress.
source: These data suggest that FMD involves unliganded ERα activation in response to shear stress.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion section as a conclusion from the experiments with exogenous estrogens and ovariectomized mice.

claim: FMD involves membrane-associated ERα.
source: The present study also showed that FMD involves membrane-associated ERα.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion section as a conclusion from the experiments with C451A-ERα and R264A-ERα mice.

claim: Membrane-associated ERα is involved in FMD.
source: The fact that FMD was similarly reduced in Esr1-/-, C451A-ERα, and R264A-ERα mice without change in receptor-dependent dilation, strongly supports that membrane-associated ERα is involved in FMD.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion section as a conclusion from the comparison of different mouse models.

claim: Flow-mediated remodeling is absent in ovariectomized rats and mice and in Esr1-/- mice.
source: Noteworthy, flow-mediated remodeling is absent in ovariectomized rats and mice and in Esr1-/- mice (Tarhouni et al., 2013) whereas this remodeling is preserved in ovariectomized rats treated with E2 (Tarhouni et al., 2014b) or resveratrol (Petit et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion section with supporting citations.

claim: Flow-mediated remodeling is preserved in ovariectomized rats treated with E2.
source: Noteworthy, flow-mediated remodeling is absent in ovariectomized rats and mice and in Esr1-/- mice (Tarhouni et al., 2013) whereas this remodeling is preserved in ovariectomized rats treated with E2 (Tarhouni et al., 2014b) or resveratrol (Petit et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion section with supporting citations.

claim: Flow-mediated remodeling is preserved in ovariectomized rats treated with resveratrol.
source: Noteworthy, flow-mediated remodeling is absent in ovariectomized rats and mice and in Esr1-/- mice (Tarhouni et al., 2013) whereas this remodeling is preserved in ovariectomized rats treated with E2 (Tarhouni et al., 2014b) or resveratrol (Petit et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion section with supporting citations.

claim: Flow-mediated remodeling requires activation of AF2 and is independent on membrane-located ERα.

evidence: This is stated in the discussion section with a supporting citation.

claim: Membrane-associated ERα is involved in NO-dependent FMD.

evidence: This is stated in the discussion section as a conclusion from the L-NNA experiments.

claim: The NO-pathway can be activated in response to receptor stimulation in C451A-ERα and R264A-ERα mice.
source: Thus, the NO-pathway can be activated in response to receptor stimulation in C451A-ERα and R264A-ERα mice, whereas only its activation by flow was reduced in these mice lacking only membrane-ERα signaling.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion section as a conclusion from the comparison of FMD and acetylcholine-mediated dilation.

claim: Only the activation of NO-pathway by flow was reduced in C451A-ERα and R264A-ERα mice lacking only membrane-ERα signaling.
source: Thus, the NO-pathway can be activated in response to receptor stimulation in C451A-ERα and R264A-ERα mice, whereas only its activation by flow was reduced in these mice lacking only membrane-ERα signaling.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion section as a conclusion from the comparison of FMD and acetylcholine-mediated dilation.

claim: Cyclooxygenase inhibition with indomethacin and EETs production inhibition with MSPPOH did not affect FMD in both WT and Esr1-/-, AF20ERα, C451A-ERα and R264A-ERα mice.
source: Nevertheless, in the present study, cyclooxygenase inhibition with indomethacin and EETs production inhibition with MSPPOH did not affect FMD in both WT and Esr1-/-, AF20ERα, C451A-ERα and R264A-ERα mice, suggesting a limited role of the pathway in mesenteric arteries of male mice.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion section as a conclusion from the indomethacin and MSPPOH experiments.

claim: The remaining FMD following the addition of L-NNA, indomethacin and MSPPOH relies probably on other hyperpolarizing agents.
source: Consequently, the remaining FMD following the addition of L-NNA, indomethacin and MSPPOH relies probably on other hyperpolarizing agents.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion section as an inference from the pharmacological experiments.

claim: Endothelium-dependent hyperpolarization (EDH) has a major role in resistance arteries homeostasis.
source: Indeed, endothelium-dependent hyperpolarization (EDH) has a major role in resistance arteries homeostasis (Brandes et al., 2000; Garland and Dora, 2017) and COX-derivatives can also induce EDH in resistance arteries and in the carotid when submitted to flow (Ohlmann et al., 2005; Bergaya et al., 2001).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion section with supporting citations.

claim: COX-derivatives can induce EDH in resistance arteries and in the carotid when submitted to flow.
source: Indeed, endothelium-dependent hyperpolarization (EDH) has a major role in resistance arteries homeostasis (Brandes et al., 2000; Garland and Dora, 2017) and COX-derivatives can also induce EDH in resistance arteries and in the carotid when submitted to flow (Ohlmann et al., 2005; Bergaya et al., 2001).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion section with supporting citations.

claim: FMD measured in the brachial artery relies mainly on the production of NO in humans.
source: In humans, FMD measured in the brachial artery relies mainly on the production of NO (Alexander et al., 2021).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion section with a supporting citation.

claim: Changes in FMD in the brachial artery predict well the endothelial dysfunction in human resistance arteries.
source: Furthermore, changes in FMD in the brachial artery predict well the endothelial dysfunction in human resistance arteries (Park et al., 2001).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion section with a supporting citation.

claim: The involvement of EDH in FMD is greater in mouse resistance arteries than in humans when measured at the level of the brachial artery.
source: As stated above, the involvement of EDH in FMD is greater in mouse resistance arteries than in humans when measured at the level of the brachial artery.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion section as a limitation of the study.

claim: A leftward shift of the flow-pressure relationship in C451A-ERα mice confirms the decreased sensitivity to flow of the resistance vasculature.

evidence: This is stated in the discussion section as a conclusion from the perfused kidney experiments.

claim: Flow activates Piezo1-dependent release of ATP through pannexin hemi-channel followed by P2Y2 activation and NO production by endothelial cells.
source: Recent studies have shown that flow activates Piezo1-dependent release of ATP through pannexin hemi-channel followed by P2Y2 activation and NO production by endothelial cells (Wang et al., 2015; Wang et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion section with supporting citations.

claim: eNOS expression level in the kidney is not altered by the absence of membrane ERα in C451A-ERα mice.

evidence: This is stated in the discussion section with a supporting citation.

claim: The reduction in NO-dependent FMD found in arteries from mice lacking membrane-ERα could be due to an excessive ROS production.
source: The reduction in NO-dependent FMD found in arteries from mice lacking membrane-ERα could be due to an excessive ROS production as the chronic treatment of C451A-ERα mice with an antioxidant treatment restored FMD to control level.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion section as a conclusion from the antioxidant treatment experiments.

claim: E2 increases the release of bioactive NO by inhibition of superoxide anion production in bovine endothelial cells.
source: This observation is in agreement with a previous work that has shown that E2 increases the release of bioactive NO by inhibition of superoxide anion production in bovine endothelial cells (Arnal et al., 1996).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion section with a supporting citation.

claim: Reducing total ROS or mitochondrial ROS production improved FMD in C451A-ERα mice.
source: Accordingly, we found that reducing total ROS or mitochondrial ROS production improved FMD in C451A-ERα mice.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion section as a conclusion from the acute antioxidant experiments.

claim: Catalase which eliminates H2O2 reduced FMD in C451A-ERα mice.
source: By contrast, catalase which eliminates H2O2 reduced FMD in C451A-ERα mice suggesting that an excessive ROS production due to the absence of membrane-associated ERα had a dual effect with (1) a reduction of NO bioavailability and (2) an increase in H2O2 production contributing to some vasodilating effect.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion section as a conclusion from the catalase experiments.

claim: An excessive ROS production due to the absence of membrane-associated ERα had a dual effect with (1) a reduction of NO bioavailability and (2) an increase in H2O2 production contributing to some vasodilating effect.
source: By contrast, catalase which eliminates H2O2 reduced FMD in C451A-ERα mice suggesting that an excessive ROS production due to the absence of membrane-associated ERα had a dual effect with (1) a reduction of NO bioavailability and (2) an increase in H2O2 production contributing to some vasodilating effect.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion section as a conclusion from the antioxidant experiments.

claim: Shear stress induces a more quiescent and less oxidative phenotype in endothelial cells.
source: Previous studies have also shown that shear stress induces a more quiescent and less oxidative phenotype in endothelial cells (Doddaballapur et al., 2015; Wu et al., 2018), thus reducing the oxidative products of mitochondrial origin.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion section with supporting citations.

claim: H2O2 could mediate FMD in human coronary arteries from patients suffering coronary artery disease although H2O2 remains deleterious.
source: Nevertheless, in a context of known dysfunctional FMD, a previous work has shown that H2O2 could mediate FMD in human coronary arteries from patients suffering coronary artery disease although H2O2 remains deleterious (Freed et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion section with a supporting citation.
